title: Executor Code Migrations
subtitle: How Executor runs code-defined data migrations exactly once
throughline: one code migration — from the registry, through the advisory lock and ledger, to its stamped completion and the R2 blobs it copies

chapters.title: The Migration Contract
chapters.blurb: Some data fixups are too big for a plain SQL file — Executor runs them as code, assembled by a tiny registry.

story.title: The Migration Contract
story.subtitle: How Executor runs code-defined data migrations exactly once

steps.title: The Migration Contract
steps.narration: Executor's cloud ships **code migrations** — one-off data fixups expressed as TypeScript, not a single SQL statement. They run through `runCodeMigrations`.
steps.say: Some changes to your data are just too big for a single SQL file. Executor writes those as code migrations, and runs them on every cloud deploy.
steps.coverSubtitle: Data fixups too big for one SQL file, written as code.

steps.title: A registry of migrations
steps.narration: On each deploy, `runCodeMigrations` asks `cloudCodeMigrations` for the list of migrations to consider.
steps.say: On each deploy, the runner asks a tiny registry for the list of migrations it should consider.

steps.title: Just a name and a run
steps.narration: Each entry satisfies one interface: a unique `name` and an async `run(context)` returning a `CodeMigrationResult` summary.
steps.say: Every migration satisfies one small contract: a unique name, and an async run function that returns a result summary.

steps.title: One migration, conditionally
steps.narration: Today the registry holds exactly one: `googleOpenApiR2BlobMigration` — and only when an `r2Bucket` is configured.
steps.say: Today that list holds exactly one migration, the Google OpenAPI blob copy, and only when a storage bucket is configured.

steps.title: Everything a run needs
steps.narration: The runner builds a `CodeMigrationContext` for every run: a `sql` handle, a `dryRun` flag, and a `log` sink.
steps.say: The runner builds a context for every run: a database handle, a dry-run flag, and a place to log.

steps.title: Run, then summarize
steps.narration: Calling `migration.run(context)` does the work and hands back a `CodeMigrationResult` whose `summary` the runner logs.
steps.say: Handing that context to the migration's run function does the actual work, and returns a summary the runner logs.

steps.title: The pieces in place
steps.narration: So the shape is set: the deploy reads the registry, gets the migration list, and is ready to hand each one a context.
steps.say: So the shape is set. The deploy reads the registry, gets the migration list, and stands ready to hand each one a context.

chapters.title: Run Once: Lock and Ledger
chapters.blurb: How the runner guarantees each migration runs exactly once, even when two deploys race.

story.title: Run Once: Lock and Ledger
story.subtitle: How Executor runs code-defined data migrations exactly once

steps.title: Run Once: Lock and Ledger
steps.narration: `runCodeMigrations` must apply each migration **exactly once**. Two guards make that true: an advisory lock and a durable ledger.
steps.say: A migration must apply exactly once, even if two deploys run at the same time. Two guards make that true: a lock, and a ledger.
steps.coverSubtitle: Exactly once, even if two deploys race.

steps.title: No duplicate names
steps.narration: First, `assertUniqueNames` walks the list and throws on any repeated `name` — names are the identity used everywhere downstream.
steps.say: First it checks the list for duplicate names, and refuses to start if it finds one. A migration's name is its identity everywhere downstream.

steps.title: One runner at a time
steps.narration: Before touching data it takes a Postgres advisory lock keyed on `executor_cloud_code_migration`, so two concurrent deploys can't both run.
steps.say: Before touching any data, it takes a Postgres advisory lock. Two concurrent deploys can't both be inside it, so nothing runs twice.

steps.title: What's already done
steps.narration: Inside the lock it reads the `cloud_code_migration` ledger — a table of completed `name`s — creating it first if needed.
steps.say: Inside the lock, it reads the ledger: a table that records the name of every migration already completed. It creates that table first if it doesn't exist.

steps.title: Skip the stamped, run the rest
steps.narration: For each migration whose `name` is in that set it logs a skip; otherwise it calls `migration.run({ sql, dryRun, log })`.
steps.say: Any migration whose name is already in that set is skipped. The rest get their run function called, one by one.

steps.title: Stamp it complete
steps.narration: When a run returns, the runner inserts the `name` plus `time_completed` into the ledger — so the next deploy will skip it.
steps.say: When a run finishes, the runner stamps the ledger with that migration's name and the time it completed. The next deploy will skip it.

steps.title: Release and return
steps.narration: In a `finally`, it releases the advisory lock and returns the list of `applied` names — the exactly-once guarantee, end to end.
steps.say: Finally, whatever happened, it releases the lock and returns the names it applied. That is the exactly-once guarantee, end to end.

chapters.title: A Migration at Work
chapters.blurb: Inside the one real migration: copying each tenant's OpenAPI spec blob to its Google twin, verified by hash.

story.title: A Migration at Work
story.subtitle: How Executor runs code-defined data migrations exactly once

steps.title: A Migration at Work
steps.narration: `googleOpenApiR2BlobMigration` copies each tenant's stored OpenAPI spec blob to a matching Google key, verifying every copy by hash.
steps.say: Here's what the one real migration actually does. For each tenant, it copies a stored spec blob from an OpenAPI key to a matching Google key, and proves every copy by hash.
steps.coverSubtitle: Copy each spec blob to its Google twin — and prove it.

steps.title: Find the rows that need it
steps.narration: `readRows` queries the `integration` table for Google Discovery sources with a non-empty `specHash` in their `config` JSON.
steps.say: It starts by querying the integration table for Google Discovery sources that carry a spec hash in their config.

steps.title: Two keys per row
steps.narration: For each row `blobKey` derives a source `o:tenant/openapi/spec/<hash>` and a target `o:tenant/google/spec/<hash>` in the R2 bucket, reached through a `wrangler` store.
steps.say: For each row it derives two object keys in the bucket: a source under the OpenAPI prefix, and a target under the Google prefix. Both are reached through a small wrangler-backed store.

steps.title: Pull the source, hash it
steps.narration: It `get`s the source blob into a temp file and computes its `sha256Buffer` — the fingerprint every later check compares against.
steps.say: It pulls the source blob down into a temporary file and hashes it. That fingerprint is what every later check compares against.

steps.title: Already copied? Compare
steps.narration: If the target key already exists, it downloads it too and compares hashes — equal means done (skip), unequal is a conflict it refuses to overwrite.
steps.say: If the target already exists, it downloads that one too and compares hashes. Equal means the work is already done, so it skips. Unequal is a conflict it refuses to overwrite.

steps.title: Copy, then read it back
steps.narration: Otherwise it `put`s the source file to the target key, `get`s it back, and throws on any `R2 round-trip mismatch` — no silent corruption.
steps.say: Otherwise it writes the source file to the target key, reads it straight back, and re-hashes. If the round-trip doesn't match, it throws. No silent corruption.

steps.title: Report the tally
steps.narration: Finally it returns a `summary`: rows seen, objects copied, targets already present — and throws if any source was missing.
steps.say: When the loop ends it returns a tally: how many rows it saw, how many objects it copied, how many targets were already present. A missing source is an error, not a shrug.

chapters.title: Dry Run, and the Whole Picture
chapters.blurb: The same path in plan mode — locking nothing, stamping nothing, changing nothing — then the full journey end to end.

story.title: Dry Run, and the Whole Picture
story.subtitle: How Executor runs code-defined data migrations exactly once

steps.title: Dry Run, and the Whole Picture
steps.narration: Pass `dryRun: true` and the same code plans the work without mutating anything — then we trace the whole journey end to end.
steps.say: There's a second way to run all of this: a dry run. The same code plans the work without changing a thing. Then we'll trace the whole journey end to end.

steps.title: No lock to take
steps.narration: On a dry run `withMigrationLock` just calls the body directly — planning never mutates, so it needn't serialize against other deploys.
steps.say: On a dry run, the runner skips the advisory lock entirely. Planning never mutates anything, so there's nothing to serialize.

steps.title: Probe, never create
steps.narration: It never runs `CREATE TABLE`; it probes with `to_regclass`, treating a missing ledger as nothing completed.
steps.say: It never creates the ledger table either. It just probes whether the table exists, and treats a missing ledger as nothing completed yet.

steps.title: Run, but stamp nothing
steps.narration: Each pending migration still runs — with `dryRun` true on its context — but afterward the runner stamps nothing.
steps.say: Each pending migration still runs, but with the dry-run flag set on its context. And afterward, the runner stamps nothing.

steps.title: Probe the blobs, copy none
steps.narration: In dry run the blob migration only calls `exists` on source and target keys — counting coverage, writing nothing.
steps.say: And the blob migration, in dry run, only asks whether each source and target object exists. It counts coverage, but copies nothing.

steps.title: How much would change
steps.narration: It reports how many objects it *would* copy, so a deploy can preview the work before committing to it.
steps.say: It reports how many objects it would copy, so a deploy can preview the work before committing to any of it.

steps.title: The whole journey
steps.narration: Apply mode, end to end: take the lock, read the ledger, run each pending migration, copy its blobs, and stamp it done.
steps.say: And here's the whole journey in apply mode. Take the lock, read the ledger, run each pending migration, copy its blobs, and stamp it done.
